It matches HNSW accuracy at 90% recall using 4 GB instead of 188 GB, at the cost of seconds-level search. The post Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab built LEANN , an open-source vector index that stores almost no embeddings. The LEANN vector index recomputes embeddings at query time instead of saving them to disk. The repo benchmark shows a 60 million chunk Wikipedia index dropping from 201 GB to 6 GB. The research paper won the Best Research Paper award at MLSys 2026 . So, it brings semantic search and RAG over personal data, on a laptop. TL;DR Size: 6 GB for 60M chunks ( repo ); 4 GB in the paper’s 76 GB Wikipedia setup. Default embedder: Contriever (110M params). It is an index, not an LLM, so no context length applies. Runs on: laptops and workstations. The paper tested an RTX 4090 box with 32 GB RAM and an M1 Ultra Mac. A CPU-only Linux install exists, with no published CPU latency. Performance: matches HNSW downstream accuracy at 90% recall, using under 5% of raw-data storage. Best: 25.5% NQ accuracy, identical to HNSW, using 4 GB instead of 188 GB. Worst: HotpotQA retrieval takes 44.80 s on the Mac, 50.1% of total pipeline time. What is LEANN? LEANN is a low-storage approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index built on top of FAISS . It targets one problem: vector indexes are often bigger than the data they index. The research paper shows a 76 GB corpus needs 173 GB of embeddings plus a 15 GB HNSW graph. That more than doubles the raw data. LEANN keeps a pruned graph, drops the full vectors, and rebuilds them on demand. The code is MIT licensed and installs with uv pip install leann . How does LEANN recompute embeddings without stalling search? Graph indexes like HNSW visit only a small set of nodes per query. LEANN exploits that. It stores the graph plus a compact product quantization (PQ) table. At query time, it re-embeds only nodes on the search path. 3 techniques keep this practical: Two-level search: cheap PQ distances rank neighbors first. Only top candidates get exact recomputation. Dynamic batching: candidates from several hops are grouped, for example 64 at once, for GPU efficiency. High-degree preserving pruning: most nodes keep few edges, while the top 2% “hub” nodes keep more. In ablations, two-level search gives an average 1.4x speedup. Adding batching raises it to 1.8x. Embedding recomputation still accounts for about 76% of query latency. How does LEANN perform on benchmarks? The research team tested NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA and HotpotQA against a 60M-passage RPJ-Wiki datastore. Latency is measured at 90% Recall@3. All figures below are self-reported in the research paper . On NQ, with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN and HNSW both reach 25.5% downstream accuracy. LEANN uses 4 GB of storage. HNSW uses 188 GB. BM25 scores 18.3%, and PQ compression scores 17.9%. The cost is search time. LEANN retrieval takes 2.48 s on NQ, versus 0.05 s for HNSW. Generation takes about 20 s, so end-to-end latency rises from 20.95 s to 23.34 s. Across datasets on the RTX 4090, LEANN retrieval ranges from 1.12 s (GPQA) to 7.12 s (HotpotQA). The IVF-based recomputation baseline, inspired by EdgeRAG , is up to 200x slower. LEANN improves exact match by up to 11.8% over BM25. The GitHub repo reports similar savings on personal data. 400K chat messages shrink from 1.8 GB to 64 MB. 38K browser entries shrink from 130 MB to 6.4 MB. LEANN vs other vector indexes Feature LEANN HNSW (FAISS) DiskANN IVF-Recompute (EdgeRAG-style) PQ compression Approach Pruned graph, recompute on demand Graph plus all vectors in RAM Graph and vectors on SSD, PQ in RAM IVF clusters, recompute on demand Compressed vectors plus graph Storage, 76 GB corpus 4 GB 188 GB 270 GB Below 5% of raw data 20 GB NQ retrieval at 90% recall (RTX 4090) 2.48 s 0.05 s 0.03 s 307.61 s Fails to reach 90% HotpotQA retrieval at 90% recall (RTX 4090) 7.12 s 0.05 s 0.11 s 429.46 s Fails to reach 90% NQ downstream accuracy (Qwen3-4B) 25.5% 25.5% Not disclosed Not disclosed 17.9% Fits 32 GB RAM workstation Yes No (OOM) Yes Yes Yes License MIT MIT MIT Not disclosed Varies by implementation Storage, latency and accuracy figures come from the LEANN paper v2 , Tables 1 and 2 and Section 7.2 (self-reported). License and design rows link to each project’s own source. Where can developers use LEANN? The repo ships ready apps for documents, Apple Mail, Chrome history, WeChat, iMessage, and ChatGPT or Claude exports. MCP readers pull live data from Slack and Twitter bookmarks. LEANN also runs as a semantic search MCP server for Claude Code . On 30 SWE-Bench Pro tasks from ContextBench, the team reports 24.2% initial relevant-code recall versus 11.4% for BM25. The agent also used 8.4% fewer tokens. HNSW is the default backend, with DiskANN for faster search. Generation works with Ollama, Hugging Face, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible API. It supports Ubuntu, Arch, WSL, macOS and Windows. Some apps, like Apple Mail search, are macOS only. Key Takeaways LEANN stores a pruned graph and recomputes embeddings at query time. 60M chunks: 201 GB down to 6 GB in the repo benchmark. Matches HNSW accuracy (25.5% on NQ) at 90% recall. Search costs seconds: 2.48 s vs 0.05 s for HNSW on NQ. MIT licensed and an MLSys 2026 Best Research Paper. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and PyPI package . It drafts 16 tokens jointly in one pass and reaches up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B. The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . TL;DR Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens. Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16. Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average. Best: 6.14x speedup on GSM8K at temperature 0 (acceptance length 7.69 tokens). Worst: 2.28x speedup on Alpaca at temperature 1. On Qwen3-4B (temperature 0), it trails DFlash on 4 of 9 tasks. What is FlashMap? FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter that maps Gaussian noise to a token block in 1 step. A small drafter proposes K tokens. The target model then checks all K in 1 parallel pass and keeps the longest matching prefix. Output stays exactly what the target would produce. Speed depends on 2 things. How many drafted tokens get accepted, and how cheaply they were drafted. EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively, so cost grows with block length. DFlash drafts the full block in 1 pass with block diffusion. Why do diffusion drafters lose acceptance? DFlash predicts each slot in the block independently. The research team calls this the factorized approximation. Picture a continuation that is “new york” or “san diego” with equal odds. An independent drafter proposes “new diego” or “san york” half the time. The target rejects those at slot 2. FlashMap builds on Flow Map Language Models . Each noise sample maps to 1 full block. The noise picks the mode for every slot jointly. How does FlashMap work? The drafter is a 6-block diffusion transformer (DiT), with embedding dimension 2048 and 16 attention heads. It reads hidden states from target layers 1, 9, 17, 25 and 33. Embedding matrix and LM head are copied from the target and stay frozen. Training runs in 2 stages: Flow teacher: a continuous flow over one-hot token blocks, trained with cross-entropy. A time reparameterization handles Qwen3’s 151,936-token vocabulary. Flow map student: semigroup distillation turns the flow into a 2-time denoiser. It jumps from noise to data in 1 step. Both drafters train on 500K samples from Open-PerfectBlend . Total compute across all models and ablations was about 4,600 GPU hours on H200s. How does FlashMap compare on benchmarks? The research team retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash on the same data and settings. Tests cover 9 benchmarks across math, code and chat, at temperatures 0 and 1. Speed: 1-step FlashMap is the fastest drafter on every Qwen3-8B task, at both temperatures. Accuracy: 1-step FlashMap beats DFlash on acceptance length in 15 of 18 settings. It has about half the parameters. Chat gains are largest: at temperature 0, gains over DFlash are 5.5% on math, 11.1% on chat. 2-step mode: acceptance length beats DFlash in 18 of 18 settings, by 10% on average. EAGLE-3: at temperature 1, it has 9% higher acceptance length but runs 35% slower. A shuffle test checks whether drafts use real inter-token structure. At 2 steps, FlashMap recovers most of the joint-structure gain of a 16-step teacher. At 1 step, it keeps only a small fraction. Drafting 4 noise samples as a tree raised speedup by 11% on average. Comparison: FlashMap vs other speculative decoding drafters Feature FlashMap DFlash EAGLE-3 DSpark Drafting style Continuous flow map, 1 or 2 passes Block diffusion, 1 pass Autoregressive, tree Semi-autoregressive Inter-token dependencies Yes, joint over block No, per-slot independent Yes, sequential Yes, lightweight sequential module Drafter size (Qwen3-8B) 500M 1B 302M (retrained, per FlashMap paper ) Not disclosed Headline claim (own source) Up to 6.1x Up to 6.17x on Qwen3-8B Up to 6.5x 60 to 85% faster per user vs MTP-1 Avg speedup, Qwen3-8B, T=0 (matched, FlashMap paper ) 4.36x 4.07x 2.55x Not tested GSM8K speedup, T=0 (matched) 6.14x 5.77x 3.20x Not tested Weights license Apache-2.0 MIT Apache-2.0 (code) Not disclosed Serving Transformers, vLLM, SGLang Transformers, vLLM, SGLang SGLang and others DeepSeek-V4 serving Average speedups are computed by Marktechpost from Figure 1(c) of the FlashMap paper. Matched rows use the authors’ retrained baselines. How do you deploy FlashMap? The flashmap package needs only torch and transformers>=4.56 . Install it with uv pip install flashmap . A spec_generate call runs drafter and target together on 1 GPU. For serving, the project page gives 2 paths: vLLM 0.31: pass the drafter in --speculative-config with num_speculative_tokens set to 16. SGLang 0.5.20: use --speculative-algorithm DSPARK with the FlashMap draft path. Set num_steps=2 to trade some speed for higher acceptance. For sampling above temperature 0, vLLM needs "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic" . Key Takeaways FlashMap drafts 16 tokens jointly in 1 pass with a continuous flow map. Up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B, using a 0.5B drafter. Faster than a retrained DFlash on all 9 Qwen3-8B benchmarks. 2-step mode keeps acceptance flat across the block. Weights are Apache-2.0, code is MIT, with vLLM and SGLang plugins. Check out the paper , project page , GitHub repo and model weights . All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. Start with work that already has a rulebook The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement. Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified. Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls. In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches. At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph. Itay Sagie , a guest contributor to Crunchbase News, is a seasoned lecturer and strategic adviser to startups and investors, specializing in strategy, growth and M&A. You can connect with him on LinkedIn for further insights and discussions. Lilly Chen was 16 and had been repeatedly hospitalized for Graves’ disease when her mother suggested they move to China and become monks. Frustrated with the care her daughter was receiving through Medicaid, she wanted to try something different. Lilly Chen, co-founder and CEO of FSH Technologies. (Courtesy photo) Chen left high school and spent about two years as a monk, ordained in the United States before spending several months at a monastery in China. She meditated, reread the same books, and gradually felt well enough to consider returning to school. She went on to enter Colorado College without a high school diploma, briefly play video games professionally, and become an engineer at Facebook . When she quit that job, she didn’t have a startup idea. She just wanted to find work she believed in. That mission eventually led her to FSH (pronounced “fish) Technologies ,” a Philadelphia-based company that’s building software for some of the government’s least glamorous tasks, including administering school food services and managing public records. After her brief stint at a large tech company, Chen realized she wanted to tackle the everyday problems that make people’s lives harder, even if solving them wouldn’t generate much excitement in Silicon Valley. “What does it actually take to solve the really unsexy, boring stuff?” she remembers asking herself. A different route to college Before Chen was thinking about government software, she was trying to get well enough to return to school. At the monastery in China, she meditated, ate food grown on-site or brought by nearby villagers, and lived without internet access. She continued taking thyroid medication and said her health became more manageable during that period. She also read. A lot. With no nearby place to buy books, she reread the ones she had brought, finding different places around the monastery to sit with them. Her attachment to those books prompted a conversation with a fellow monk who asked what she enjoyed about reading and where she might find more books. The discussion eventually turned to colleges, and why she wasn’t attending one. Chen explained her health problems. He observed that she seemed well. She realized she was. So Chen returned to the U.S., homeschooled herself and enrolled at Colorado College without having earned a high school diploma. Today, we help 25,000 Shopify brands simplify gnarly workflows like inventory, bundling, and order fulfillment (for even the world's largest brands like Sennheiser, Godiva, YAMAHA, and Stanley Drinkware). Tomorrow, we'll deliver intelligent automation that feels like an on-site operations team so merchants can focus on building their brand.</p> <p>We're a fully-remote and bootstrapped company with teammates around the world. We love what we do and love who we build for. We're a small team of 9 (3 Support specialists) who amplify each other's work by working closely together: dev with support, support with marketing, and so on. We're curious, kind, scrappy yet rigorous, and highly intentional. If this sounds like the type of team you'd like to be a part of, we'd love to hear from you.</p> <h2>About this role</h2> <p>In this role, you'll have significant ownership of your work, make impactful decisions daily, and report directly to the founders. This is a full-time remote position open to candidates in all timezones.</p> <p>Support is the foundation of everything we do. Our apps have consistently maintained high ratings on the Shopify App Store because our support team genuinely cares about helping merchants succeed. As one of our early support hires, you'll get to know our products inside and out and become a go-to expert on how things work under the hood.</p> <p>We hire slowly and keep the bar high, so the people you work with every day will be some of the best you’ve worked with. You'll be joining a small but growing support team, where we all wear many hats. You'll need strong troubleshooting instincts, a curious mind, and a willingness to get into the weeds. You should feel comfortable making judgment calls on UX or product questions, and know when something needs to be escalated. There's plenty of room to grow with us.</p> <h2>What we're looking for</h2> <ul> <li>Somone who fixes the process while you’re fixing the ticket.</li> <li>Someone who's comfortable diving into technical issues and can confidently support merchants over email and through clear, helpful video recordings.</li> <li>A strong track record in customer-facing roles, with a focus on delivering thoughtful, efficient support. You listen closely, ask the right questions, and know how to turn a frustrating situation into a positive experience.</li> <li>Good judgment around what needs to be escalated and what doesn't. You'll know when to loop in teammates and how to make that handoff seamless for the merchant.</li> <li>An eye for patterns and the ability to turn merchant feedback into actionable insights for our product and engineering teams.</li> <li>The ability to prioritize effectively. You can assess what's urgent, what's important, and what can wait, especially when everything feels like it needs attention.</li> <li>Comfort with change. You stay calm when the product evolves and enjoy picking up new knowledge as you go.</li> <li>A team-first mindset. You jump in to support others, document what you've learned, and share what's working so we can all move faster together.</li> <li>Strong communication skills, especially in writing. You know how to keep things clear, friendly, and easy to follow, whether you're talking to a merchant or a teammate.</li> <li>Natural troubleshooting instincts. You enjoy working on tricky issues and figuring out what's actually going on, not just treating the symptoms.</li> <li>Great attention to detail. You care about getting the small things right, because they add up to a better experience.</li> <li>A curious mind. You're always learning, always testing, always a few steps ahead.</li> <li>The ability to explain complex ideas in a simple way, especially for merchants who aren't technical.</li> </ul> <h2>Experience</h2> <ul> <li>Previous experience in technical support at a SaaS or tech company</li> <li>Familiarity with HelpScout or other ticketing systems</li> <li>Hands-on knowledge of front-end development (HTML, CSS, browser dev tools)</li> <li>Working understanding of REST APIs and common data formats like JSON or XML</li> <li>Comfort with debugging using Chrome DevTools, especially for browser or front-end issues</li> <li>Knowledge of how HTTP and DNS work</li> <li>Experience reading API documentation and troubleshooting third-party integrations or custom app setups</li> <li>Some exposure to GraphQL APIs</li> </ul> <h2>Bonus experience</h2> <ul> <li>Shopify theme development and Liquid: Knowing how themes interact with app blocks, line item properties, and cart/checkout logic helps when diagnosing visual or UX issues on merchant stores.</li> <li>Understanding of Shopify's admin and storefront APIs: Familiarity with how Shopify's APIs behave (especially in headless or custom setups) can be useful when troubleshooting sync issues, metafields, or app-triggered updates.</li> </ul> <h2>Beyond expertise, success in this role means embodying 3 core values</h2> <ol> <li><strong>Resourcefulness:</strong> You're relentlessly resourceful and always find ways to achieve the highest standards of quality. You know where to look and whom to consult when faced with challenges.</li> <li><strong>Ownership:</strong> You take complete ownership and pride in your work. This means deeply understanding our existing and prospective merchants, as well as our product.</li> <li><strong>Communication:</strong> You're clear, thoughtful, and intentional in how you communicate with both merchants and teammates. You surface issues early, share relevant context, and keep things moving without needing constant follow-up.</li> </ol> <h2>We're async by default</h2> <p>If you've ever ended a day of back-to-back meetings wondering when you were supposed to get any actual work done, we get it. We've been there. We've built a culture that protects time, encourages focus, and trusts you to do great work without constant check-ins.</p> <p>We meet once a week for 30 min on Mondays. The rest of the time, we default to async: clear Slack threads, thoughtful Looms, and shared docs.</p> <h2>Perks &amp; compensation</h2> <ul> <li>Competitive salary + annual pay increases.</li> <li>$1,000 annual workspace stipend for laptop, headphones, or that standing desk you've been eyeing.</li> <li>Flexible hours. Work when you're most productive. We just ask for ~4 hours of overlap with Eastern Time (9 am to 5 pm EST).</li> <li>Flexible vacation policy. Take the time you need, no arbitrary caps.</li> </ul> <h2>Our inter

It drafts 16 tokens jointly in one pass and reaches up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B. The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . TL;DR Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens. Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16. Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average. Best: 6.14x speedup on GSM8K at temperature 0 (acceptance length 7.69 tokens). Worst: 2.28x speedup on Alpaca at temperature 1. On Qwen3-4B (temperature 0), it trails DFlash on 4 of 9 tasks. What is FlashMap? FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter that maps Gaussian noise to a token block in 1 step. A small drafter proposes K tokens. The target model then checks all K in 1 parallel pass and keeps the longest matching prefix. Output stays exactly what the target would produce. Speed depends on 2 things. How many drafted tokens get accepted, and how cheaply they were drafted. EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively, so cost grows with block length. DFlash drafts the full block in 1 pass with block diffusion. Why do diffusion drafters lose acceptance? DFlash predicts each slot in the block independently. The research team calls this the factorized approximation. Picture a continuation that is “new york” or “san diego” with equal odds. An independent drafter proposes “new diego” or “san york” half the time. The target rejects those at slot 2. FlashMap builds on Flow Map Language Models . Each noise sample maps to 1 full block. The noise picks the mode for every slot jointly. How does FlashMap work? The drafter is a 6-block diffusion transformer (DiT), with embedding dimension 2048 and 16 attention heads. It reads hidden states from target layers 1, 9, 17, 25 and 33. Embedding matrix and LM head are copied from the target and stay frozen. Training runs in 2 stages: Flow teacher: a continuous flow over one-hot token blocks, trained with cross-entropy. A time reparameterization handles Qwen3’s 151,936-token vocabulary. Flow map student: semigroup distillation turns the flow into a 2-time denoiser. It jumps from noise to data in 1 step. Both drafters train on 500K samples from Open-PerfectBlend . Total compute across all models and ablations was about 4,600 GPU hours on H200s. How does FlashMap compare on benchmarks? The research team retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash on the same data and settings. Tests cover 9 benchmarks across math, code and chat, at temperatures 0 and 1. Speed: 1-step FlashMap is the fastest drafter on every Qwen3-8B task, at both temperatures. Accuracy: 1-step FlashMap beats DFlash on acceptance length in 15 of 18 settings. It has about half the parameters. Chat gains are largest: at temperature 0, gains over DFlash are 5.5% on math, 11.1% on chat. 2-step mode: acceptance length beats DFlash in 18 of 18 settings, by 10% on average. EAGLE-3: at temperature 1, it has 9% higher acceptance length but runs 35% slower. A shuffle test checks whether drafts use real inter-token structure. At 2 steps, FlashMap recovers most of the joint-structure gain of a 16-step teacher. At 1 step, it keeps only a small fraction. Drafting 4 noise samples as a tree raised speedup by 11% on average. Comparison: FlashMap vs other speculative decoding drafters Feature FlashMap DFlash EAGLE-3 DSpark Drafting style Continuous flow map, 1 or 2 passes Block diffusion, 1 pass Autoregressive, tree Semi-autoregressive Inter-token dependencies Yes, joint over block No, per-slot independent Yes, sequential Yes, lightweight sequential module Drafter size (Qwen3-8B) 500M 1B 302M (retrained, per FlashMap paper ) Not disclosed Headline claim (own source) Up to 6.1x Up to 6.17x on Qwen3-8B Up to 6.5x 60 to 85% faster per user vs MTP-1 Avg speedup, Qwen3-8B, T=0 (matched, FlashMap paper ) 4.36x 4.07x 2.55x Not tested GSM8K speedup, T=0 (matched) 6.14x 5.77x 3.20x Not tested Weights license Apache-2.0 MIT Apache-2.0 (code) Not disclosed Serving Transformers, vLLM, SGLang Transformers, vLLM, SGLang SGLang and others DeepSeek-V4 serving Average speedups are computed by Marktechpost from Figure 1(c) of the FlashMap paper. Matched rows use the authors’ retrained baselines. How do you deploy FlashMap? The flashmap package needs only torch and transformers>=4.56 . Install it with uv pip install flashmap . A spec_generate call runs drafter and target together on 1 GPU. For serving, the project page gives 2 paths: vLLM 0.31: pass the drafter in --speculative-config with num_speculative_tokens set to 16. SGLang 0.5.20: use --speculative-algorithm DSPARK with the FlashMap draft path. Set num_steps=2 to trade some speed for higher acceptance. For sampling above temperature 0, vLLM needs "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic" . Key Takeaways FlashMap drafts 16 tokens jointly in 1 pass with a continuous flow map. Up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B, using a 0.5B drafter. Faster than a retrained DFlash on all 9 Qwen3-8B benchmarks. 2-step mode keeps acceptance flat across the block. Weights are Apache-2.0, code is MIT, with vLLM and SGLang plugins. Check out the paper , project page , GitHub repo and model weights . TL;DR Size: 2 stacks, 17 skills (15 from Ronny, 2 from Jiachen), 5 checklists, 5 companion notes. Runs on: Any machine running MiniMax Code (Node.js 22.19+) or Claude Code. No GPU. Skills are plain Markdown. Performance: No benchmarks or eval results published. Best: long-command-check , a 10-point audit for long shell commands and background tasks. We just open-sourced MCode Stack: the actual workflows and skills the MiniMax Code team uses every day to build MiniMax Code. https://t.co/vREt7i8m2M — RonnyHe (@Ronny_MiniMax) October 28, 2026 What is MiniMax MCode Stack? MCode Stack is an open-source repo of agent skills from MiniMax’s MiniMax Code team. MiniMax Code is the MiniMax’s open-source terminal coding agent, also MIT-licensed. The stack holds no MiniMax Code source code. It holds only workflows, skills and checklists. The repo pairs with a column called MCode Engineering Notes . Each note explains one idea. The repo makes that idea runnable. Published notes cover subagents , tool context , compaction versus memory and long bash commands . A note on per-turn context tax is marked upcoming. What skills are inside Ronny’s stack? MiniMax’s stack ships 15 skills, grouped by moment in the working day: Plan and split (3): subagent-split-check , engineering-small-prs , engineering-change-descriptions . Context and tools (2): tool-budget-audit , context-tax-audit . Long sessions and commands (3): long-session-check , handoff-doc , long-command-check . Review (4): independent-review , engineering-code-review , engineering-review-comments , engineering-review-feedback . Experiments and hotfixes (3): harness-experiment , trajectory-review , engineering-emergency-changes . A few ideas stand out. independent-review gives the reviewer exactly 3 inputs: the diff, the requirement and test results. It deliberately withholds the author’s conversation. The reasoning: a reviewer inheriting the author’s context repeats the author’s blind spots. subagent-split-check says to split work only when context is the measured problem. Splitting by team or question type is not a valid reason. tool-budget-audit separates 2 costs: tool definitions and tool results. Tool search mainly cuts the first. Programmatic tool calling mainly cuts the second. harness-experiment enforces 1 change per experiment. It tracks flipped tasks, requests per task, tokens, cache hit rate and wall-clock time. The long-command checklist has 10 items. It asks whether moving a command to background re-runs the process. It also asks whether unread results survive compaction. The 6 engineering-* skills are adapted from Google Engineering Practices . That material stays under CC-BY 3.0, per the stack’s NOTICE . How do you install MCode Stack? There are 3 paths, per the README : One skill: clone the repo and copy a skill folder into ~/.agents/skills/ . Whole stack as a local plugin: copy stacks/ronny into MiniMax Code’s local plugin directory. Marketplace: in MiniMax Code desktop, add the MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack marketplace. This option is rolling out gradually. The same catalog works in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack . MiniMax Code also reads ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ . The skills use the common SKILL.md format, so most work in other agents that support skills. How does MCode Stack compare with other skill packs? The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . TL;DR Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens. Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16. Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average. Best: 6.14x

The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph. Itay Sagie , a guest contributor to Crunchbase News, is a seasoned lecturer and strategic adviser to startups and investors, specializing in strategy, growth and M&A. The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels. Rebekah Johnson, founder and CEO of Numericle. (Courtesy photo) The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation. The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected. Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents. Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one, fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers. For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning. Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone. From a regulatory warning to a company Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West , said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission ’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016. She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling. About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen. “Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking. Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle. She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes. “When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said. That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A. Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare. The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers. Verifying increasingly convincing fakes Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls. Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers. A business call from Numeracle, delivered with name, logo, and reason for calling. (Photo courtesy of Numeracle) Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam. AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles. “The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.” She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail. Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort. The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call. Investor POV: ‘Doing more with less’ For Lenard Marcus , a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers. He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.” Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales. Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said. “She’s sales. The post MiniMax Open-Sources MCode Stack: 15 Agent Skills Its Coding Team Uses Daily appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> MiniMax has open-sourced MCode Stack , the workflows and agent skills its team uses to build MiniMax Code. The MiniMax MCode Stack agent skills went public on October 28, 2026 under the MIT license . It is not a prompt collection. Each piece is a SKILL.md skill or checklist that installs directly into MiniMax Code . For developers, it turns harness engineering habits into steps an agent can actually run. TL;DR Size: 2 stacks, 17 skills (15 from Ronny, 2 from Jiachen), 5 checklists, 5 companion notes. Runs on: Any machine running MiniMax Code (Node.js 22.19+) or Claude Code. No GPU. Skills are plain Markdown. Performance: No benchmarks or eval results published. Best: long-command-check , a 10-point audit for long shell commands and background tasks. We just open-sourced MCode Stack: the actual workflows and skills the MiniMax Code team uses every day to build MiniMax Code. https://t.co/vREt7i8m2M — RonnyHe (@Ronny_MiniMax) October 28, 2026 What is MiniMax MCode Stack? MCode Stack is an open-source repo of agent skills from MiniMax’s MiniMax Code team. MiniMax Code is the MiniMax’s open-source terminal coding agent, also MIT-licensed. The stack holds no MiniMax Code source code. It holds only workflows, skills and checklists. The repo pairs with a column called MCode Engineering Notes . Each note explains one idea. The repo makes that idea runnable. Published notes cover subagents , tool context , compaction versus memory and long bash commands . A note on per-turn context tax is marked upcoming. What skills are inside Ronny’s stack? MiniMax’s stack ships 15 skills, grouped by moment in the working day: Plan and split (3): subagent-split-check , engineering-small-prs , engineering-change-descriptions . Context and tools (2): tool-budget-audit , context-tax-audit . Long sessions and commands (3): long-session-check , handoff-doc , long-command-check . Review (4): independent-review , engineering-code-review , engineering-review-comments , engineering-review-feedback . Experiments and hotfixes (3): harness-experiment , trajectory-review , engineering-emergency-changes . A few ideas stand out. independent-review gives the reviewer exactly 3 inputs: the diff, the requirement and test results. It deliberately withholds the author’s conversation. The reasoning: a reviewer inheriting the author’s context repeats the author’s blind spots. subagent-split-check says to split work only when context is the measured problem. Splitting by team or question type is not a valid reason. tool-budget-audit separates 2 costs: tool definitions and tool results. Tool search mainly cuts the first. Programmatic tool calling mainly cuts the second. harness-experiment enforces 1 change per experiment. It tracks flipped tasks, requests per task, tokens, cache hit rate and wall-clock time. The long-command checklist has 10 items. It asks whether moving a command to background re-runs the process. It also asks whether unread results survive compaction. The 6 engineering-* skills are adapted from Google Engineering Practices . That material stays under CC-BY 3.0, per the stack’s NOTICE . How do you install MCode Stack? There are 3 paths, per the README : One skill: clone the repo and copy a skill folder into ~/.agents/skills/ . Whole stack as a local plugin: copy stacks/ronny into MiniMax Code’s local plugin directory. Marketplace: in MiniMax Code desktop, add the MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack marketplace. This option is rolling out gradually. The same catalog works in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack . MiniMax Code also reads ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ . The skills use the common SKILL.md format, so most work in other agents that support skills. How does MCode Stack compare with other skill packs? Feature MiniMax MCode Stack anthropics/skills obra/superpowers Publisher MiniMax Code team Anthropic Jesse Vincent (obra), Prime Radiant License MIT; engineering-* skills CC-BY 3.0 Apache 2.0 for many skills; document skills source-available MIT Skill count 17 (15 + 2) Not disclosed 15 listed in README Focus Harness engineering, review, context budgets, long sessions Creative, development, enterprise, documents Brainstorming, planning, TDD, subagent-driven development, debugging Agents named MiniMax Code, Claude Code Claude Code, Claude.ai, Claude API 16 harnesses, incl. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI Claude Code install /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack /plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official Published evals Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed MCode Stack is narrower than both. It targets people who design agent harnesses, not only people who use agents. Superpowers covers far more harnesses today. Key Takeaways MiniMax open-sourced 17 SKILL.md skills and 5 checklists under MIT. Skills pair with MCode Engineering Notes, turning essays into runnable checks. independent-review feeds a reviewer only the diff, requirement and test results. Installs into MiniMax Code or Claude Code via a plugin marketplace. No published evals yet, so treat it as a playbook, not proof. Check out the GitHub repo and MiniMax Code . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. It drafts 16 tokens jointly in one pass and reaches up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B. The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . TL;DR Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens. Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16. Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average. Best: 6.14x
newContent: MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ An Artificial Intelligence News Platform Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:48:40 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.marktechpost.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cropped-Favicon-512-x-512-1-1-32x32.png MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ 32 32 127842392 Google DeepMind Introduces Gemini 4 Carbon, Its Top Model for Cyber Defense and Coding https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/10/28/google-deepmind-gemini-4-carbon-frontier-model/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:48:38 +0000 https://www.marktechpost.com/?p=83665 Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model that scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro. Access starts with vetted cyber defenders, at $2/$10 per million tokens. The post Google DeepMind Introduces Gemini 4 Carbon, Its Top Model for Cyber Defense and Coding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Carbon , its strongest model to date. Gemini 4 Carbon is a frontier model from Google built for long-horizon agentic coding and cybersecurity defense. It ranks #1 on the updated v5.0 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59. For developers, the catch is access. Carbon starts with a vetted group of cyber defenders, not the public API. TL;DR Size: Parameter count and context window not disclosed. Its predecessor, Gemini 4 Argon , has a 1,048,576-token context. Runs on: Google-hosted only. No open weights, no self-hosting, no quantized variants. Performance: Leads 15 of 17 published benchmarks versus Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1. Best: 96.2% BFS F1 on GraphWalks (256K to 1M tokens), versus 84.2% for Argon. Worst: 81.5% on OSWorld-2.1, trailing Claude Opus 5.5 at 87.2%. Bottom line: Best: state-of-the-art vulnerability finding, exploitation and patching. Worst: you probably cannot call it yet. What is Gemini 4 Carbon? Carbon is the second Gemini 4 model, following Gemini 4 Argon . Google team states that the model targets hard, long-running engineering work. Internal teams saw Carbon run for days on single tasks. Examples include root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Google also tuned Carbon for full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. On WebDev Arena , Carbon gained 89 Elo points to reach #4 at 1769. How does Gemini 4 Carbon perform on benchmarks? Google published a 17-row comparison in its launch post . Carbon was run at the highest thinking setting. Most rival numbers are self-reported by each provider, per Google’s evaluation methodology . Agentic coding : Carbon scores 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (AA), ahead of Opus 5.5 at 59.6%. It hits 9.6% on SWE-sweep, narrowly ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 9.5%. On FrontierSWE, GPT-6 Astra leads at 65.5% versus Carbon’s 61.2%. Computer use and knowledge work : Carbon reaches 77.4% on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1. On Vending-Bench 2, it ends with a $16,484 bank balance, the highest listed. Long context and science : GraphWalks is the widest gap: 96.2% versus 71.8% for GPT-6 Astra. Carbon also posts 80.0% on RiemannBench. Why does Carbon relevant for cybersecurity? Google frames Carbon around the full defense lifecycle: find, validate, then fix. Cyber benchmarks were evaluated without guardrails. Finding: 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , versus 85.4% for GPT-6 Astra. Exploiting: 54.8% on ExploitGym , versus 42.4% for GPT-6 Astra and 34.5% for Opus 5.5. Patching: 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , versus 68.0% for Argon and GPT-6 Astra. Google computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym scores itself, using its Antigravity harness. ExploitGym ran with mitigations off. Internally, Carbon showed more than 2x higher success at generating secure code than Argon.
